prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I move my preferred configuration from B016 to B018. Five of eight members place it in their top three and it is ranked by all eight, which counts for little by itself, but the reasons behind that support are substantive. Kane and Mele supplied a clean theoretical result (the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal), and Molenkamp's group tested it in a well-defined material, HgTe/CdTe quantum wells, by observing helical edge transport. A prediction matched by decisive experiment on a specific system is the kind of discovery the prize is meant to recognise. The concept has been confirmed independently for about two decades, including ARPES on three-dimensional materials, and it is not premature. As an experimentalist I value that the experiment is more than a confirmation, because the edge-channel conductance measurement was the first realisation of a new phase of matter.
statement.case_against: The credited trio gives an incomplete history. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum-well realisation that guided Molenkamp's experiment, and Zhang's death means he cannot be honoured, which makes any allocation of the experimental credit delicate. The three-dimensional topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others) lies close to the boundary of the citation. The 2016 prize for topological phases and transitions may also make some members see the area as partly honoured. If the committee judges that an incomplete allocation is unfair, B041 is the cleaner two-name configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B018 first, calls the idea clean and a prediction promptly realised in nature, and notes that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D topological-insulator discoverers are outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree on both the merit and the maturity, and I changed my own ballot partly because of your argument. I would qualify the claim that the prediction was promptly realised. The experiment followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, not Kane and Mele directly, and that is the weakest link in the attribution. I suggest we frame the citation around the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators, and that we state openly that the 3D materials work is not what the prize recognises. Whether that boundary survives the 3D discoveries is not something I can settle from the file.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks DMFT (B009) first and B018 fourth, treating B018 as workable but an incomplete account of the history because Zhang is deceased and Bernevig and Hughes are not credited.
responses.response: I share your reservation about the history, and I think the committee should weigh it more heavily than the opening rankings do. I part ways with you on B009. DMFT is a very important method, but you yourself raise whether a theoretical method counts as a discovery in the sense of the will, and the accuracy for real materials depends on solver choices and double-counting. I do not find that a stronger case than a predicted and observed phase of matter. I would be interested in how you see the experimental falsifiability of DMFT claims, since that is where my instincts as an experimentalist diverge from yours.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock (B041) first, stresses that the two-name credit fits a prize cleanly, and argues that progress is limited by what can be measured and how accurately.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case and I take it seriously. A precision instrument at the 1e-18 level with independent labs reproducing it is close to my own idea of an experimental achievement, and the clean two-name credit is a real advantage over B018. My reservations are that Hall, Hansch and Wineland were recognised in 2005 and 2012 for adjacent technology, and that the redefinition of the second is still pending. I rank it as the first alternative. If the committee decides the attribution problem in B018 is disqualifying, I would move to B041 without hesitation.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B030) first as a clean theory-plus-experiment prize built on a simple continuum model, and sees B018 second and very mature.
responses.response: I agree that B030 has an attractive theory-plus-experiment structure. I would hold it back for now. The main experiments date from 2018, the superconducting pairing mechanism and the correlated phases are still debated, and sample-to-sample twist-angle disorder complicates reproducibility. Eriksson and Lindroth make the same point about timing. B018 has the advantage of two decades of stable interpretation, which makes it the lower-risk choice this year, and B030 can wait without losing its case.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B020) first, argues it is distinct from the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and discloses that she knows several of the people involved.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure. I accept that circuit QED is a distinct discovery from the 2025 work and that it is mature. My difficulty is practical: four credited names against a three-person limit, with Girvin the one omitted, and a prize in superconducting circuits so soon after 2025 invites criticism of the committee. That does not make the science weaker, but it makes the timing and the attribution harder than for B018. I would put it behind both B018 and B041.

uncertainties: Whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be justified in the citation, or whether it makes the three-name configuration unfair.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases weighs against recognition of this separate discovery.
Whether a prize bounded by the 2D quantum spin Hall effect can avoid the priority disputes over 3D topological insulators.
I rely on recollection of the priority history and have not verified it independently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B018 or the alternatives B041 and B016. My astroparticle background could incline me towards B016, my first-ranked opening choice, but my documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH) do not include IceCube or any named candidate.
